name: Why AI Projects Stall
blurb: The evidence on what makes AI projects fail.
title: Why AI Projects Stall
answer: Most failed AI projects fail for organisational reasons rather than technical ones. RAND's interview study found leadership related causes were cited most often, and Gartner predicted at least 30 percent of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, citing poor data, risk controls, cost and unclear value.

crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Most failed AI projects fail for organisational reasons, not technical ones, with leadership causes cited most often in RAND's interview study.

That is the pattern across both sources here. RAND's practitioners pointed at leadership rather than model performance. Gartner's forecast of at least 30 percent of generative AI projects abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025 rests on poor data, risk controls, cost and unclear value, which are also organisational conditions rather than capability limits.

For AI specifically this matters because the binding constraint is usually assumed to sit elsewhere. Compute, buildings and power determine what can be trained and served, but they do not determine whether a deployed project survives contact with a business. A stalled project consumes the same scarce accelerators and the same scarce power as one that ships, so failure at the organisational layer is also a waste of the physical layer.

The data does not say which organisations failed, in which sectors, or at what rate outside the Gartner forecast. It covers two sources, one an interview study and one a prediction, and the prediction had not yet resolved at the time of writing. Nothing here measures compute, data centre capacity or electricity, so the link to infrastructure is inference from the fact that stalled projects still draw on it, not something these numbers establish.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

A small, scoped test validating technical feasibility before larger investment. It answers "can this work," which is a different question from "will this work here," the question the pilot must answer next.

Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

Whether the information an AI use case relies on is reliable enough for the task: accurate, current, consistent, and owned. It requires practical internal controls, not a data science team or enterprise warehouse.

sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences leader

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Research on failed AI projects points to recurring causes: leaders not defining the problem clearly or misunderstanding what AI can do, poor or unavailable data, insufficient infrastructure to deploy models, and applying AI to problems too hard for current methods. Analysts have also warned that many generative AI pilots are abandoned after proof of concept because costs, risks or value were unclear.

In life sciences the regulated environment adds validation and data governance hurdles that can stall promising pilots. Projects that succeed define a business outcome, secure an executive owner, confirm data availability and quality early, plan validation from the start, and decide in advance what success at scale looks like.
